title: Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?
core_idea: This topic introduces the move from average change over an interval to change at a single instant. A limit describes what average rates approach as the interval around the instant shrinks.
what_students_need_to_understand: This is the conceptual bridge into derivatives. BC students will keep using this limiting idea later for motion, parametric curves, polar change, and series approximations.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by recognizing whether a question asks about an interval or an instant and by connecting the instant case to limiting behavior.
answer_move: Ask: over an interval or at one point? If it is at one point, describe the instantaneous rate as the value approached by average rates over smaller intervals.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Ask: over an interval or at one point? If it is at one point, describe the instantaneous rate as the value approached by average rates over smaller intervals. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by recognizing whether a question asks about an interval or an instant and by connecting the instant case to limiting behavior.
common_point_loss: Trying to compute an instantaneous rate as a direct quotient with zero change in x.

title: Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation
core_idea: A limit describes the value a function approaches as x gets close to a chosen input. Limit notation names that approaching behavior precisely.
what_students_need_to_understand: Limit notation is the language used for continuity, derivatives, infinite behavior, improper integrals, and series convergence claims.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by reading and writing the approaching input, function, direction when specified, and value approached.
answer_move: Read the notation as: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L. Keep approaches separate from equals.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Read the notation as: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L. Keep approaches separate from equals. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by reading and writing the approaching input, function, direction when specified, and value approached.
common_point_loss: Replacing the limit with f(a) automatically, or dropping the direction marker on a one-sided limit.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Graphs
core_idea: A graph can show what y-value a function approaches as x moves toward a chosen input from the left, right, or both sides.
what_students_need_to_understand: Graph-based limits train students to focus on nearby behavior instead of point values, a skill that returns in continuity, asymptotes, derivative graphs, and polar/parametric contexts.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by identifying left-hand and right-hand behavior and concluding whether the two-sided limit exists.
answer_move: Trace the graph toward the x-value from both sides before looking at the point on the graph.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Estimating Limit Values from Graphs. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Trace the graph toward the x-value from both sides before looking at the point on the graph. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by identifying left-hand and right-hand behavior and concluding whether the two-sided limit exists.
common_point_loss: Using a filled or open point as the limit value without checking nearby graph behavior.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Tables
core_idea: A table can suggest a limit by showing how function values behave for x-values close to a chosen input.
what_students_need_to_understand: Tables appear when exact formulas are not given, and BC students also use tabular evidence later for rates, accumulation, and convergence reasoning.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by using nearby table values from both sides and writing an estimate that matches the evidence.
answer_move: Look inward from both sides of the table, then state the trend and estimated limit.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Estimating Limit Values from Tables. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Look inward from both sides of the table, then state the trend and estimated limit. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by using nearby table values from both sides and writing an estimate that matches the evidence.
common_point_loss: Choosing one table entry instead of describing the trend across nearby entries.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits
core_idea: Limit properties let students combine simpler limits to determine limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and composite functions.
what_students_need_to_understand: This is where limits become a reliable calculation tool instead of only a graphical or numerical idea.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by applying a valid property, preserving expression structure, and showing setup that makes the final value follow.
answer_move: Break the expression into parts, determine component limits, then apply the matching property.

common_point_loss: Applying quotient or composition rules mechanically when the needed conditions are not met.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation
core_idea: Some limit expressions hide their behavior until they are rewritten into an equivalent useful form.
what_students_need_to_understand: Factoring, rationalizing, simplifying, or using identities can turn a blocked expression into a solvable limit, including forms that later resemble BC improper-integral and series work.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by choosing a valid rewrite, showing the transformed expression, and evaluating from the simplified form.
answer_move: When substitution is blocked, ask what equivalent form removes the obstacle.

weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: When substitution is blocked, ask what equivalent form removes the obstacle. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by choosing a valid rewrite, showing the transformed expression, and evaluating from the simplified form.
common_point_loss: Stopping at 0/0, or canceling terms that are not common factors.

title: Selecting Procedures for Determining Limits
core_idea: This topic is about choosing the method that fits the limit problem before carrying out the calculation.
what_students_need_to_understand: AP questions often reward recognizing the right path: direct property use, graph or table reasoning, factoring, rationalizing, one-sided analysis, or later L'Hospital's Rule.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by classifying the problem form and selecting a procedure that matches it.
answer_move: Before solving, name the cue: direct substitution works, sides must be checked, factoring helps, or another strategy fits.

title: Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem
core_idea: The squeeze theorem finds a limit by trapping one function between two functions that approach the same value.
what_students_need_to_understand: This is an early example of theorem-based limit reasoning where conditions force a conclusion, which is useful again in BC convergence and approximation arguments.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by showing bounds, showing both bounding limits match, and then stating the squeezed conclusion.
answer_move: Write the inequality first, find the outside limits, then conclude the middle limit.

weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Write the inequality first, find the outside limits, then conclude the middle limit. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by showing bounds, showing both bounding limits match, and then stating the squeezed conclusion.
common_point_loss: Naming the theorem without showing the bounding relationship and matching limits.

title: Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits
core_idea: The same limit can be represented by notation, words, a graph, a table, or an equation.
what_students_need_to_understand: AP Calculus regularly changes representation without changing the underlying mathematical claim, and BC adds more representations later through parametric, polar, and series contexts.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by identifying the same limiting behavior across representations and keeping the claim consistent.
answer_move: Convert each representation into: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L.

weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Convert each representation into: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by identifying the same limiting behavior across representations and keeping the claim consistent.
common_point_loss: Matching a table or graph to a function value instead of to approach behavior.

title: Exploring Types of Discontinuities
core_idea: A discontinuity is a place where continuity fails. The type depends on whether the value, one-sided limits, or bounded behavior fails.
what_students_need_to_understand: Naming the type helps students explain what failed rather than merely saying the graph is broken.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by classifying the discontinuity and connecting that classification to limit evidence.
answer_move: Check left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and f(c), then classify based on which part fails.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Exploring Types of Discontinuities. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Check left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and f(c), then classify based on which part fails. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by classifying the discontinuity and connecting that classification to limit evidence.
common_point_loss: Calling every gap removable or every discontinuity an asymptote without checking behavior.

title: Defining Continuity at a Point
core_idea: A function is continuous at a point when f(c) exists, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(c).
what_students_need_to_understand: Continuity is a condition checklist used before applying theorems in derivatives, integrals, differential equations, and BC series-related function work.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by checking all three conditions and using them to justify whether the function is continuous.
answer_move: Use the checklist: value exists, limit exists, value equals limit, then state the conclusion.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Defining Continuity at a Point. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Use the checklist: value exists, limit exists, value equals limit, then state the conclusion. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by checking all three conditions and using them to justify whether the function is continuous.
common_point_loss: Saying a function is continuous because the graph looks connected without verifying conditions.

title: Confirming Continuity over an Interval
core_idea: Continuity over an interval means the function is continuous at every point in that interval.
what_students_need_to_understand: Many AP conclusions depend on interval-level continuity, including theorem use, domain reasoning, accumulation, and convergence-adjacent function claims.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by identifying the interval, checking special points, and naming domain restrictions or endpoints that matter.
answer_move: Start with the function family and domain, then check special points inside the interval.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Confirming Continuity over an Interval. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Start with the function family and domain, then check special points inside the interval. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by identifying the interval, checking special points, and naming domain restrictions or endpoints that matter.
common_point_loss: Claiming continuity over an interval while ignoring holes, asymptotes, piecewise boundaries, or excluded domain values.

title: Removing Discontinuities
core_idea: A removable discontinuity can be fixed by defining or redefining the function value so it equals the limit at that point.
what_students_need_to_understand: This topic turns the definition of continuity into an action: find the value or parameter that makes the function continuous.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by finding the relevant limit and setting the function value or parameter equal to it.
answer_move: Find the limit at the discontinuity first, then set f(c) or the parameter expression equal to that limit.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Removing Discontinuities. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Find the limit at the discontinuity first, then set f(c) or the parameter expression equal to that limit. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by finding the relevant limit and setting the function value or parameter equal to it.
common_point_loss: Solving for a value without showing that it matches the limiting behavior.

title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
core_idea: An infinite limit describes function values growing without bound as x approaches a finite input.
what_students_need_to_understand: Students need to distinguish unbounded behavior from finite limits, jumps, and ordinary function values; BC later reuses unbounded behavior in improper integrals.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by using limit notation to describe unbounded behavior and connecting it to a vertical asymptote when appropriate.
answer_move: Check each side of the input. If f(x) grows without bound, write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Check each side of the input. If f(x) grows without bound, write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by using limit notation to describe unbounded behavior and connecting it to a vertical asymptote when appropriate.
common_point_loss: Writing only does not exist when the problem asks for behavior or an asymptote connection.

title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
core_idea: A limit at infinity describes end behavior as x grows very large positive or negative.
what_students_need_to_understand: End behavior helps students describe long-run function behavior analytically, graphically, verbally, and later in BC convergence contexts.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by identifying end behavior, writing the correct limit at infinity, and connecting a finite result to y = L.
answer_move: Ask what f(x) approaches as x goes far left or far right. If it approaches L, name y = L.
mini_example_question: A calculus prompt asks you to justify a conclusion involving Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes. What should your work and sentence make clear?
weak_answer: I would write the final value or conclusion without showing why it follows.
point_attaining_answer: Ask what f(x) approaches as x goes far left or far right. If it approaches L, name y = L. Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by identifying end behavior, writing the correct limit at infinity, and connecting a finite result to y = L.
common_point_loss: Confusing vertical asymptotes with horizontal asymptotes or finite-input limits with limits at infinity.

title: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem
core_idea: The Intermediate Value Theorem says a continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values somewhere inside the interval.
what_students_need_to_understand: This is an early existence theorem: it proves a value occurs without finding its exact location, a style of reasoning BC students will keep using in more advanced settings.
how_this_becomes_points: You earn points by verifying continuity, showing the target value lies between endpoint values, and stating the existence conclusion.
answer_move: Write the conditions first: continuous on [a,b], target between f(a) and f(b), therefore some c exists in (a,b).

point_attaining_answer: Write the conditions first: continuous on [a,b], target between f(a) and f(b), therefore some c exists in (a,b). Then make the scoring connection explicit: You earn points by verifying continuity, showing the target value lies between endpoint values, and stating the existence conclusion.
common_point_loss: Jumping to the conclusion without verifying continuity and the endpoint-value condition.
